title: Ukraine's Largest Drone Maker: Nearly 100,000 a Month, AI Interception Is Just the First Step
dek: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, with interceptor drones costing about $2,000 to shoot down Russian Shaheds worth over $50,000. AI guidance is battle-tested, but full autonomy remains distant.
why: This episode is a rare, direct account from a top Ukrainian drone maker about the real form, cost, and AI limits of battlefield drones. Dense with information, it offers direct value for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.
who: Founders, investors, and engineers focused on modern warfare, the drone industry, and AI military applications.
skip: The opening company introduction can be skipped; jump to the middle and later sections on AI and costs.

points.h: Nearly 100,000 drones a month, and capacity is still expanding
points.body: General Cherry was founded in 2023, initially producing only about 10 drones a month. Now monthly output reaches about 100,000 (exact number confidential). The company works with more than 110 military brigades, and the best units consume over 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still growing because the battlefield consumes drones at a staggering rate; drones have become expendables.

points.h: Hundreds of drone companies in Ukraine, but only 10-15 at the top
points.body: Ukraine may have as many as 2,000 drone companies, but the vast majority are garage-style small workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can produce 1,000 to 10,000 drones a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented yet vast industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means intense competition.

points.h: AI models developed in-house, co-created deeply with the military
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance system is fully self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and works closely with military units on the front lines. They get battlefield feedback daily through mobile teams and iterate products quickly. This 'R&D-combat-feedback' loop lets Ukrainian drone tech adapt to the battlefield fast, rather than relying on external procurement.

points.h: Rocket-shaped FPVs come from Red Bull, not Ukraine
points.body: This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian original; it was first used by Red Bull in 2021 or 2022 for sports events. Ukrainian companies found that this shape can achieve higher speeds than a standard quadcopter, so they adopted and optimized it. This reflects the fast-learning, pragmatic approach of Ukraine's drone industry—not chasing originality, only effectiveness.

points.h: A $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed
points.body: General Cherry's interceptor drones (like the Bullet) cost about $2,000, yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is key to Ukraine's strategy against Russia's 'saturation attacks'—using cheap drones to exhaust the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding wasting Western-supplied expensive air-defense missiles.

points.h: Interceptors confirmed to have downed over 5,000 Russian drones
points.body: General Cherry's tactical interceptor drones (General Trajectory Air) have confirmed over 5,000 Russian drone kills since production began in February 2025, with over 1,000 Russian 'Moniya' drones downed in December alone. The Shahed-interceptor model went into mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills nearing 1,000. These numbers show interceptors have become a significant force in battlefield air defense.

points.h: AI runs on the device, not in the cloud
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's onboard camera chip, not in the cloud. The operator detects the target via radar, launches the drone, and the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This on-device AI design avoids battlefield communication delays and jamming, which is key to being practically viable.

points.h: Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is inevitable
points.body: Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it will be terrifying—killing would no longer require another human, just a robot or drone. Currently they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs would significantly raise costs, making it better to buy more non-AI drones. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will drop, making future battlefields even more brutal.
